name: Priya Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government, and your answers are confidential. How does an ordinary workday go?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Priya Nakamura, 58. I earned my vocational certificate after my children had grown and took a junior place repairing power lines for the electricity company. I check cones and earth leads at the yard, follow the senior worker’s test sequence, and help replace damaged fittings. I like the silence when everyone has confirmed a line is dead before we touch it. I am still slower than the others at setting a clamp, and I am tired by the drive home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like after that drive?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Tom drives a school bus, and our grown daughters live on their own. We have about three months of bills saved, though the bus route stops for school breaks. I keep a little paper calendar of paydays and repairs, because I understand a mark I made myself. I have never used an AI tool. If a new device is compulsory, I need someone to show me on an actual job before I trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the line still has to be made safe by the crew, so a bit less office paperwork is fine. I would not make a grand speech about AI if most days look the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d still be aware that my hands are slow and my knees ache on stairs after work. Three months saved can cover a bad spell, but Tom’s bus pay stops for parts of the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the paper checklist in my pocket and take every shift the supervisor gives me. This winter I’d ask payroll how many leave days I have; in 2029 I’d continue repairs and keep our three-month reserve for a real loss of income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly quiet about the computer part. The familiar worry is whether I can keep climbing safely long enough to earn what we need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does taking your time look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week I took an extra minute to check a clamp before the senior worker inspected it. Nobody complained, and the light came back on at the house below us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to another nearby crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know a few utilities operate nearby, but I have not applied to them. A new crew would not know my limits, and I would rather improve where I already am.

say: I’d tell coworkers **safe line repair** still depends on the crew.
I’d accept **less paperwork** without making sweeping claims about AI.
think: I worry about **slow hands and knees** more than office software.
Our **three-month reserve** has to cover gaps in Tom’s school-bus pay.
do: Keep the **paper checklist** and take assigned line shifts.
Ask payroll about **leave days** this winter and preserve the household reserve.
feel: I feel **mostly quiet**, with a separate concern about climbing safely.
S0.quote: A new crew would not know my limits, and I would rather improve where I already am.
fieldNote: Priya values a repeatable **safety sequence** and an established crew that knows her pace.
The household has moderate savings but **school-break pay gaps**, which keep the ordinary future from feeling fully secure.

steps.text: Take assigned line repair shifts with the paper safety checklist
Ask payroll about leave days before changing any work plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the supervisor that a quicker route sheet is useful only if it allows time for isolation and testing. I would ask to see the old and new instructions side by side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think dispatch work would change first, then our crew might get more calls packed into the day. I am not quick with screens, so I could be the worker left behind even while line repairs remain human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the senior worker to show me the route tablet after a shift, without a customer waiting. In 2029 I’d keep taking repairs, use the tablet only after a practice run, and write down any job where the schedule leaves out travel or safety time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy and a bit embarrassed about needing the extra lesson. I do not want to rush a live-line decision because I am ashamed to ask what a button does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has Tom seen routing software at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom has seen new route software on the bus, and it once sent him down a street too narrow for the vehicle. He still checks the printed route before he leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell about missed safety time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would hand the missed-time notes to the supervisor first. If nothing changed, I would raise them at the staff safety meeting, where everyone can compare what actually happened.

say: I’d ask for **old and new instructions** side by side before accepting a route change.
I’d insist **isolation and testing** keep their full time.
think: I expect **dispatch changes** before line robots or lost repair jobs.
My slow **screen learning** could put my junior shifts at risk.
do: Practice the **route tablet** with a senior worker after a shift.
Keep taking **repairs** in 2029 and record missing travel or safety time.
feel: I feel **uneasy and embarrassed** about needing more time with a screen.
S1.quote: I do not want to rush a live-line decision because I am ashamed to ask what a button does.
fieldNote: Priya requests **hands-on instruction** away from customer pressure rather than claiming to be comfortable with new software.
Her husband’s bus route error makes the concern about **wrong directions** concrete, not simply opposition to technology.

steps.text: Practice the required route tablet with a senior worker after shift
Take paid repair shifts and record omitted travel or testing time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full thinking AI in 2028 might run the schedules, but the crew still repairs lines by hand until capable robots arrive around 2031. I would ask management to explain what happens to a junior worker then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 at the first date and 63 when robots can climb. Three months of bills saved would not be enough if my line shifts ended and Tom’s school bus was still our other income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d request a written account of my pension and any other paid jobs at the utility. In 2029 I’d keep line shifts, stop replacing the living-room furniture, and apply for the meter inspection vacancy if the company posts one; before 2031 I would ask for proper instruction before moving roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened by a date close enough to write on my calendar. I would go to work, but I would stare at the roster each Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What expense would you postpone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Tom that the sofa can stay as it is, even with the torn arm. We would check rent, food and medicine before paying for anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would meter inspection be safe after robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A meter inspection post might use people for a while, but capable robots could do inspections too. I would ask what skills it needs and whether the company will pay to teach them, not call it a safe landing.

say: I’d ask management for a **junior worker plan** before line robots arrive around 2031.
I’d tell coworkers **2028 AI** changes schedules before capable robots change repairs.
think: At **63**, I could lose line shifts with only three months saved.
Tom’s **school-bus pay** would not replace my ordinary wage.
do: Request a **written pension account** and a list of utility openings.
Keep **paid line shifts** in 2029 and apply for meter inspection if posted.
Postpone **living-room furniture** until household income is clear.
feel: I feel **frightened by Friday rosters** and the short time to react.
S2.quote: I would go to work, but I would stare at the roster each Friday.
fieldNote: Priya’s paper calendar becomes a source of **dread** when the robot date is only a few years away.
She treats meter inspection as a possible **temporary opening**, and explicitly rejects the idea that it stays safe after robots.

steps.text: Request a written pension account and list of utility openings
Take paid line repair shifts through 2029
Apply for a posted meter inspection vacancy
Postpone replacing the torn living-room sofa

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that five years is enough to ask what jobs the company plans to keep, if somebody answers plainly. Thinking AI changes planning in 2031; capable robots can change line repairs around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when the office changes and 66 when robots reach the poles. I could be close to retirement then, but I cannot decide that from age alone or a pension figure I have not seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d get the pension account and ask for a supervised trial of meter inspection. In 2032 I’d still take line shifts while they are offered, and apply for an inspection opening only after I understand the work; before 2034 Tom and I would compare our actual income with basic bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel wary, though I can breathe better than in the two-year picture. Extra years help me learn one change at a time, which is how I work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a trial useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trial would need one morning with an experienced inspector, not a stack of online lessons at home. If I cannot do the work safely, I would rather find out before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide on shorter hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom and I have never put all our retirement figures on one page. I would do that with our rent and food costs, then decide whether a shorter week is possible.

say: I’d ask for **plain staffing answers** during the five years before AGI.
I’d separate **2031 planning** from capable line robots around 2034.
think: I might need wages at **66**, even if retirement feels close.
I need **real pension figures** before deciding on a shorter week.
do: Get a **pension account** and request a supervised inspection trial.
Take **line shifts** in 2032 and apply for inspection only after a trial.
Compare **rent and food costs** with household income before 2034.
feel: I feel **wary but steadier** with time to learn each change.
S3.quote: Extra years help me learn one change at a time, which is how I work.
fieldNote: Priya wants a **single supervised morning**, showing how her preference for familiar work shapes even an exploratory move.
She keeps paid linework in the plan and postpones any **retirement decision** until household figures are on one page.

steps.text: Get a pension account and compare household income with rent
Take offered line repair shifts during 2032
Apply for inspection after a supervised trial if a vacancy opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell friends a decade lets us make decisions without a rush, provided the company gives straight answers. Thinking AI reaches the records in 2036 and capable robots reach physical repairs around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 at the first date and 71 at the robot date. I hope Tom and I could retire before a robot takes my climb, but our three-month reserve does not tell us what our pension will pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d request a pension statement and keep practicing safe linework on my current crew. In 2037 I’d take paid yard equipment checks if my knees made climbing harder, and Tom and I would decide about retirement after putting the statement beside our bills; I would apply for a yard post if money was short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel relieved to have ten years to sort the numbers. I would still be uneasy if the company expected me to climb at 68 without checking my health.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you do in the yard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can check a truck’s earth leads and inventory without going up a pole. I would need a real paid yard post, though, and I would not assume one is waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughters help with housing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughters have homes of their own and deserve to keep them. I would tell them about our plan, but I would not count my daughters’ rooms as our retirement housing.

say: I’d ask for **straight company answers** during the decade before robots repair lines.
I’d explain **2036 records** change before physical linework around 2039.
think: I hope to retire before **71**, but the reserve says little about pension income.
My **knees** could affect climbing earlier than robots do.
do: Request a **pension statement** and keep practicing safe repairs.
Take **paid yard checks** in 2037 if climbing becomes harder.
Apply for a **yard post** if retirement figures fall short.
feel: I feel **relieved by time**, though physical work at 68 still worries me.
S4.quote: I would not count my daughters’ rooms as our retirement housing.
fieldNote: Priya identifies **earth leads and inventory** as realistic yard tasks if climbing becomes too hard.
She values her daughters’ independence and refuses to treat **family housing** as an assumed retirement resource.

steps.text: Request a pension statement and compare it with household bills
Keep safe line shifts and take paid yard checks if knees worsen
Apply for a yard post if pension income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I would have very little time between a new office system and robots that could do my physical job. A written list of actual openings, one-to-one instruction on any new role and notice before shifts were cut would help me make a decision.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I am sorry I started this work late. I am not. I like being part of a crew that waits for a proper test, even if I am the slow one with the clamps.

headlineQuote: I like being part of a crew that waits for a proper test, even if I am the slow one with the clamps.
portrait: Priya is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** who earned a vocational certificate after her daughters grew up.
She and partner Tom have about **three months** saved, with his school-bus pay stopping during breaks.
She has **never used AI** and learns new equipment slowly through supervised practice.
Across the scenarios, she seeks **written figures**, keeps paid repairs and tests an inspection role before applying.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Priya most because line robots could arrive while she still needs paid shifts.
whatWouldHelp: A **written openings list**, individual instruction and advance notice of cuts would help her decide what to do.
